references.text: Matthew's parallel account of the temptation, where the devil shows Jesus all the kingdoms of the world and their glory and offers them to him in exchange for worship.
Jesus calls Satan 'the ruler of this world,' which corresponds with the devil's claim to have power over the kingdoms of the world.
Jesus refers to the devil as 'the ruler of this world,' consistent with Satan's claim that the authority of the world has been handed over to him.
Paul describes Satan as 'the ruler of the powers of the air,' confirming the devil's claim to hold a form of dominion over this world.
Paul calls Satan 'the god of this age,' reflecting the devil's claim to have been given authority and glory over the kingdoms of the world.
John writes that 'the whole world lies in the power of the evil one,' which mirrors the devil's claim of power over the world.
The dragon (Satan) gives the beast his power, his throne, and great authority—a parallel to the devil's claim that he can give power to anyone he wishes.
In Daniel it is said that the Most High rules over the kingdom of men and gives it to whom he wills—a contrast to the devil's claim that this authority has been handed over to him.
'The earth and everything in it belongs to the Lord'—showing that God is the true owner of the world, contrary to the devil's claim.
Paul teaches that all authority comes from God, correcting the devil's claim that power has been given to him alone.
